item.title: Experience AI begins reaching classrooms across Latin America
item.dc:creator: Saúl Maldonado
item.description:

The post Experience AI begins reaching classrooms across Latin America appeared first on Raspberry Pi Foundation.
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this year, we announced that we’re expanding Experience AI, our AI literacy programme, across Latin America to bring AI education to nine more countries through support from Google.org. Working with local partner organisations, we offer Experience AI training and resources that teachers can use to enable young people to learn a foundational understanding of AI technologies, their social and ethical implications, and the role that AI can play in their lives.

Over the past few months, Experience AI launch events have already taken place in Brazil, Chile, Argentina, and Mexico. At every event, we met educators, policymakers, universities, non-profit organisations, and technology leaders and explored how AI literacy can become part of classrooms across their country. Experience AI brought us all together around a shared goal: giving teachers the confidence and resources they need to help young people understand and engage with AI critically and responsibly.

Growing the Experience AI partner network in Latin America

Across Latin America, the local organisations we are partnering with to implement Experience AI bring deep expertise in teacher professional development and education. Partners include Fundación Sadosky in Argentina, Fundación Kodea in Chile, Sincroniza Educação in Brazil, and Educación para Compartir in Mexico. 

Each partner is implementing the programme in a way that reflects its local education system and context. We work with them individually and also facilitate their collaboration around shared challenges.

A delivery model designed for lasting impact across Argentina

In Argentina, Experience AI was officially launched in June during a Google event in Buenos Aires.

Our Argentinian partner Fundación Sadosky is taking a distinctive approach to Experience AI teacher professional development by working through a network of public universities across the country, rather than relying on a central training team. Through this approach, Experience AI training will reach educators in diverse regions across the country as Fundación Sadosky builds on local expertise and existing educational networks.

Growing local capacity and developing regional trainers means Experience AI will make a lasting impact for teachers and learners, enabling high-quality AI education long after the programme’s first rollout.

The first cohort of participating universities is now working with teachers across several Argentinian provinces, before the programme expands nationwide. Experience AI aims to support around 1,700 secondary school teachers and reach an estimated 153,000 students.

Turning vision into action

It’s been very rewarding coming together with local partners, Google.org, universities, and education communities across Latin America around our shared vision of high-quality AI education for all young people.

After the launch events, the focus now turns to practical action: supporting teachers and bringing Experience AI into classrooms across the region. 

As the programme grows, we also look forward to working with new partners across Latin America to bring AI literacy to even more educators and young people. By 2028, we and our Latin American partners aim to support 24,000 more educators and reach more than 1.25 million young people through Experience AI.

item.title: Celebrating the UK’s National Engineering Day 2026
item.dc:creator: Philippa Hanman
item.description:

The post Celebrating the UK’s National Engineering Day 2026 appeared first on Raspberry Pi Foundation.
item.content:encoded:
We’re celebrating National Engineering Day in the UK with our friends at the Royal Academy of Engineering. National Engineering Day aims to make the UK’s engineers and engineering more visible, and celebrate how they improve everyday lives and shape the world around us.

Now hiring: The engineers of 2076

This year, the Royal Academy of Engineering is marking its 50th anniversary by looking 50 years into the future. Through job ads for roles that don’t exist yet, they invite us to imagine the engineering careers that will build life on the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Scientific investigations in space

Some of those future engineers could be taking their first steps today. They might be getting their first experience with space science in the European Astro Pi Challenge, for example. This ESA Education project is run in collaboration with the Raspberry Pi Foundation and offers young people the amazing opportunity to conduct scientific investigations in space by writing computer programs that run on Raspberry Pi computers aboard the International Space Station (ISS). 

We spoke to Geraint Ballinger, a Software Development and Deployment Engineer who works on the Astro Pi Challenge, to find out what engineering roles he thought could be important in the future. We also discussed how the engineers of 2076 need opportunities to experiment, solve problems, and build confidence today.

Hi Geraint. Can you tell us a bit about your role as a Software Development and Deployment Engineer at the Raspberry Pi Foundation?

I like to describe it as a blend between traditional software engineering and teaching. The overall aim of my work is to help young people run code on the Astro Pi computers aboard the International Space Station, which means designing systems that hide unnecessary complexity so students can learn and solve problems effectively, while ensuring the software deployed to orbit remains secure and compliant.

Part of the role is to create applications and code libraries that young people can use to simplify the routine things so they can focus their energy on the interesting aspects of running code in space: taking pictures of the Earth and investigating various scientific concepts. I also oversee the pipeline that receives their work — reviewing submissions, moderating Mission Zero images, and building internal tools to streamline the review process.

On the flight software side, I am jointly responsible for delivering the Astro Pi operating system on the ISS. This involves preparing and delivering system updates, coordinating security reviews, and developing internal astronaut-facing applications such as the application used by the astronauts to focus the Astro Pi cameras.

What do you most enjoy about your role?

I enjoy the sheer variety of engineering challenges to which I am exposed. In any given week, I might be writing a Python library, developing a Typescript web application, or diagnosing a low-level hardware failure on the ISS — like debugging corrupted SD cards.  In particular, I have really enjoyed the challenge of maintaining a system on real physical hardware in space. Operating a Raspberry Pi in orbit makes it impossible to ignore the physical machine: you have to actively design around constraints such as solar radiation, tight power and bandwidth budgets, and hardware degradation over the mission lifecycle.  It’s been really interesting to learn about the procedures and processes involved in delivering software and hardware into orbit.

How does your work help young people’s Astro Pi programs run on the ISS?

I developed the Astro Pi Replay tool, an online browser emulator that simplifies testing and code submission for Mission Space Lab. This allows anyone with a standard school laptop to test their code as if it were running on the ISS, without the need for physical hardware.

Alongside the software tooling, I am also involved in writing the educational materials that guide young people and mentors through the core concepts required for Mission Space Lab.  These resources hopefully enable participants to get up to speed quickly, and to produce working code within a few hours.

What skills do you see young people practising through Astro Pi that future space engineers will need?

Problem-solving, patience, critical thinking, and creativity are vital skills for future space engineers that young people put into practice through the Astro Pi Challenge.

In Mission Space Lab, the more advanced of the Astro Pi missions, young people learn to break down complex tasks into manageable pieces and to coordinate independent pieces of work as a team.

Becauses technical failures and software bugs are inevitable realities of operating in space, Mission Space Lab gives participants practical opportunities to hone their debugging skills, to build resilience and a constructive approach to problem-solving, and foster an active curiosity about underlying system processes.

National Engineering Day is imagining the engineers of 2076. What space engineering job would you invent, and what would someone need to know or be able to do to succeed in it?

I’d invent the role of Interplanetary Communications Manager. If we’ve reached Mars by 2076, then keeping a reliable link back to Earth will be critical infrastructure, and someone will need to look after it.

The job would sit across software and hardware. Software will be a big part of it, but you’d always be working with physical systems, particularly radio transmission. I don’t think we’ll find a fundamentally new way to communicate across space, so I’d expect the role to build on radio and optical technology we already use today. So the key knowledge would be the physics of communication, such as how radio waves and light travel over huge distances, along with how networks are designed to stay reliable.

I also expect AI to touch almost every area of engineering, but I doubt something this critical (and expensive!) would be left entirely without human oversight. There will always be a need for people who truly understand how the system works and can judge whether it can be trusted. That understanding is what I’d want a candidate to bring to the role.

Thanks, Geraint! And we hope any future Interplanetary Communications Managers try out the Astro Pi Challenge, which is open for submissions now!

Get involved with National Engineering Day

Now it’s your turn. What engineering role would you create for 2076? Find out more about how to take part on the Royal Academy of Engineering website.  

And if your young people and future engineers would like to enter the European Astro Pi Challenge 26/27, visit: astro-pi.org to select a mission.

The post Celebrating the UK’s National Engineering Day 2026 appeared first on Raspberry Pi Foundation.

item.title: That’s a wrap! Coolest Projects 2026
item.dc:creator: Helen Gardner
item.description:
There are a few Coolest Projects events still to come in the Coolest Projects 2026 cycle, but we are already getting ready to kick off Coolest Projects 2027. Before we do, we’re taking a  look back at some of the incredible things the young tech creators in the global Coolest Projects community have achieved this…

The post That’s a wrap! Coolest Projects 2026 appeared first on Raspberry Pi Foundation.
item.content:encoded:
There are a few Coolest Projects events still to come in the Coolest Projects 2026 cycle, but we are already getting ready to kick off Coolest Projects 2027. Before we do, we’re taking a  look back at some of the incredible things the young tech creators in the global Coolest Projects community have achieved this year, both through the online showcase and at in-person events around the world. 

More than 15,000 young people from 40 countries shared over 4500 creations in the Coolest Projects online showcase. The Coolest Projects team hosted events in the UK, Ireland, India, and two locations across the US, while our partners brought creators together at in-person events in a further 11 countries, with events in Malaysia, South Africa and Argentina still to come.

With young people sharing their brilliant ideas, ambitious projects, and creativity with the world, 2026 has been a year to remember, and we can’t wait to see what comes next!

But don’t just take our word for it — hear from members of the Coolest Projects community about their experiences too.

From the community

For some, the events are about celebrating a shared passion for making with family and friends.

“I went to Coolest Projects last year with my cousins and thought it was cool, so I wanted to apply this year. I was very late applying so only had 3 days to create a project before the deadline. It was pretty intense! My highlight was being at the event with my cousin, Noah. It was great fun!” – Leo, creator, Coolest Projects Ireland

It’s not just creators who enjoy being part of the community. Mentors take away lasting impressions and a feeling of connection too.

“We usually avoid competitions because coding’s about curiosity, creativity, and sharing knowledge, not racing against each other. But Coolest Projects is completely different: it’s like one big party where everyone’s invited to share what they’ve made. We’re so grateful Project Code Cloud got to be part of it.” – Dannielle, Coolest Projects mentor, Australia

We are also very thankful to our VIP judges, who encourage and give feedback to creators both in the online showcase and at in-person events. Ben, a VIP judge for the online showcase, shared some powerful advice with creators:

“Keep building. Keep experimenting. Keep trying things. […] Always stay curious. Always try to stay learning. […] And the most important thing is it’s OK to fail. Trying new things is difficult and you’re always going to make mistakes, but that’s the best way to learn.” – Ben Powley, Senior Developer, Jagex

Catch up on the livestream to hear advice and feedback from all the VIP judges involved in the online showcase this year and check out their favourite projects.

Some more highlights from 2026

A judge who’s been in their shoes

Akari, a 16-year-old CoderDojo member from Japan who has showcased her own projects at Coolest Projects seven times, joined us as a VIP judge for the online showcase. We were delighted that young creators could hear a genuine peer voice on the panel, alongside industry judges, offering inspiration and encouragement.

This year’s Broadcom Coding with Commitment® recipient

The Broadcom Coding With Commitment® award is a special recognition for a creator who uses coding to support their community through a project that aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. In this year’s online showcase, the award went to Egehan from Türkiye, for their Scratch project Viridia — Back to the World, an educational game that teaches players about water conservation. Egehan shared some thoughts about the challenges they faced while building it:

“Writing the code I used to create the 3D visuals for this game was a bit of a challenge for me. I would often dream about the mathematical calculations required for the code (which, to be honest, was quite interesting).” – Egehan

Partner events around the globe

With 14 partner events due to have taken place around the world by the end of 2026, more creators than ever before have been able to share their projects and connect with a like-minded community locally. Here are a few highlights from the events.

The first event of the year was Coolest Projects Belgium, which took place in March and was organised by CoderDojo Belgium. Ruhee, Global Partnerships Coordinator at the Raspberry Pi Foundation, who attended the event, was particularly impressed by Zeno and Lukas’s Orbitol 6 project, a three-axis robotic arm they’ve been developing for several years, with plans to take it from three axes to six in the future! She also highlighted Jack’s Moppentrappen, a joke-telling project that uses AI to replicate Jack’s voice, allowing it to tell jokes in French as well as English.

Coolest Projects Japan, organised by CoderDojo Japan, was also held in March and welcomed 79 entries, which you can explore here.

Coolest Projects Sudan, organised by Orientations Training Centre, ran for the second time this year. The event was held in Egypt and was designed to provide a safe and accessible space for young Sudanese people affected by displacement. Among the projects on display was an AI-based fruit freshness detector, built by 7-year-olds Khalid and Nour.

“This showcase reflects our belief that Sudan’s future depends on empowering young people to learn, create, and solve problems. We are committed to building the opportunities and platforms they need to shape a better future for Sudan.” – Abbdelmoneim M. Ahmed, CEO, Orientations Training Centre

Looking ahead to 2027

We are excited to share that the Coolest Projects 2027 online showcase will open for entries in January, and the Coolest Projects online showcase celebration will take place on 23 June. 

We’ll also be running in-person Coolest Projects events in Ireland, the UK, India, the US, South Africa, and Kenya next year, with further in-person events due to be run by partners around the world. We will announce the full calendar of in-person events soon. 

You can already save the date for:

Coolest Projects Belgium — 13 March 2027

Coolest Projects USA Minnesota — 17 April 2027

Coolest Projects Ireland — 24 April 2027 at Explorium, Dublin

Coolest Projects UK Bradford — 15 May 2027 at Life Centre, Bradford

Coolest Projects USA Georgia — 15 May 2027

Coolest Projects UK Cardiff — 22 May 2027 at Wales Millennium Centre, Cardiff

Coolest Projects global showcase celebration — 23 June 2027, online

If you would like to be first to hear news and dates for the 2027 online showcase and in-person events, sign up to our newsletter or follow the Coolest Projects social channels (find us on LinkedIn, Facebook, and Instagram).

The post That’s a wrap! Coolest Projects 2026 appeared first on Raspberry Pi Foundation.

item.title: Reintroducing Code Classroom – now with the Blocks editor
item.dc:creator: Mel Farrington
item.description:
Code Classroom — formerly known as the Code Editor for Education — is our free, safe tool for teaching and learning computing and programming. We’re delighted to share that Code Classroom now includes our new Blocks editor, based on the open-source Scratch editor. With the Blocks editor, Code Classroom offers the familiar creative programming experience…

The post Reintroducing Code Classroom – now with the Blocks editor appeared first on Raspberry Pi Foundation.
item.content:encoded:
Code Classroom — formerly known as the Code Editor for Education — is our free, safe tool for teaching and learning computing and programming. We’re delighted to share that Code Classroom now includes our new Blocks editor, based on the open-source Scratch editor.

With the Blocks editor, Code Classroom offers the familiar creative programming experience used by millions of young learners worldwide, plus all its helpful features for teachers. You can now inspire learners’ imagination and build their confidence through drag-and-drop coding in the same tool over 4500 schools already use to teach Python and web development. 

Early feedback on this Code Classroom addition has been very encouraging. One UK computer science teacher told us:

“I think it’s going to be hugely transformative for schools… Not just Scratch. Python, HTML and CSS… all in one platform is enormous.”

Bartholomew Owuor, a computer science  teacher at Cathsam School in Kenya said:

“When the coding blocks were introduced, I was able to widen my scope and to include so many learners from different ages.”

All Code Classroom features, including the Blocks editor, are now also available when you use Experience CS.

Made for the classroom

Code Classroom is built for schools and shaped by real teacher feedback. Every feature is designed around how teachers and students actually work.

  • Free forever: Completely free to use, with no hidden costs or subscriptions
  • Private by default: A secure environment designed for schools’ needs
  • Built-in classroom / learning management: Create classes, assign work, and track learner progress in one simple platform

Up and running in minutes

There’s no software to install and nothing for your school’s IT team to manage. Code Classroom runs in the browser, so you can set up your classes, add your students, and be ready to teach by your very next lesson.

Code Classroom is now also integrated with Google Classroom. That means you can import your existing classes with just a few clicks, which reduces setup time. With Google single sign-on for students, everything stays connected and easy to manage. You can spend less time on administration and more time on teaching.

Three ways to learn, one platform

  • Blocks editor: Where young people can drag and drop colourful blocks to code games, stories, and animations, learning core programming concepts without needing to type
  • Python editor: Where learners can move from typing their very first text-based program all the way to the skills and confidence to write and understand code
  • Web editor: Where young people can design and build their own web pages with text-based HTML and CSS

With all three editors in one place, you can support every student, whatever their coding experience.

 I want to create my free school account

item.title: Preparing young people for frontier technologies: Our new partnership with the UK government
item.dc:creator: Dan Fisher
item.description:
Around the world, governments are grappling with the same question: how do you prepare young people for careers shaped by emerging technologies? In the UK, part of the answer is TechFirst, and we’re proud to be playing a central role in it. Through the new TechFirst partnership with the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and…

The post Preparing young people for frontier technologies: Our new partnership with the UK government appeared first on Raspberry Pi Foundation.
item.content:encoded:
Around the world, governments are grappling with the same question: how do you prepare young people for careers shaped by emerging technologies? In the UK, part of the answer is TechFirst, and we’re proud to be playing a central role in it.

Through the new TechFirst partnership with the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), we are expanding Ada Computer Science, the free computing education platform we have built with the University of Cambridge for UK students and teachers. It’s one of the ways the UK government plans to bring frontier tech education to a million secondary students (11- to 18-year-olds) over the next three years.

What’s happening in the UK

TechFirst is the UK government’s £187 million tech skills initiative, designed to open up pathways into the country’s tech sector. It supports people at every stage, from students in school to university researchers and career changers.

Backed by major tech employers, the programme focuses on six frontier technologies: cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, engineering biology, semiconductors, and advanced connectivity technologies.

Ada Computer Science sits at the heart of TechFirst’s schools strand. With DCMS funding, we’re adding new content and features to the platform, and everything stays completely free.

For the first time, Ada Computer Science now covers ages 11 to 19, with new teaching and learning materials for 11- to 14-year-olds added alongside everything we already offer for ages 14 to 19. Thanks to the new materials, students can start exploring computing and frontier technologies earlier, and build on that learning all the way through to the end of secondary education.

Alongside the expansion of the Ada CS platform, DCMS is funding Regional Delivery Partners to bring hands-on technology activities into secondary schools across the UK, giving students practical experience and a real sense of where a tech career could take them.

Beyond the economic opportunities that understanding frontier technologies opens up for young people, gaining this knowledge and skills helps young people have agency and power in a world where technology plays an ever greater role in their lives.

We are pleased to offer the new frontier technologies materials, like all our teaching and learning resources, at no cost to teachers and students. This is one way in which we support equal access to a high-quality computing and AI education for all young people.

What’s coming next

We will add new content and features to Ada CS in phases, including:

  • Learning content on artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, quantum computing, engineering biology, semiconductors, and advanced connectivity technologies
  • Learning content designed specifically for 11- to 14-year-olds, covering a wide range of computing topics and building digital literacy
  • Interactive student challenges and self-paced projects
  • Careers content, including real-life case studies
  • Links to workshops, events, and activities run by Regional Delivery Partners

Find out more

If you’re a teacher or student in the UK, you can explore the first TechFirst content release on the Ada Computer Science website. Create a free account to be first to hear about the new content and features.

The post Preparing young people for frontier technologies: Our new partnership with the UK government appeared first on Raspberry Pi Foundation.

Blythe brings a wealth of experience to our governance at a time when our mission to enable all young people to realise their full potential through the power of computing…

item.content:encoded:
I am delighted to share the news that Blythe Masters has been appointed as the next Chair of the Raspberry Pi Foundation’s Board of Trustees. Blythe brings a wealth of experience to our governance at a time when our mission to enable all young people to realise their full potential through the power of computing and AI has never felt more urgent.

Blythe is one of the most prominent figures in global financial services and fintech. A graduate and Senior Scholar of Trinity College, University of Cambridge, she spent nearly three decades at JPMorgan, rising to its Executive Committee and holding senior leadership roles including Chief Financial Officer of the Investment Bank and Head of Global Commodities. After leaving JPMorgan in 2014, Blythe served as CEO of Digital Asset and later became a Founding Partner at Motive Partners, the fintech-focused investment firm. Most recently, Blythe served as Group CEO of FNZ, the global wealth technology platform and Motive Partners portfolio company.

Blythe has extensive corporate governance experience, currently serving as the Chair of JPMorgan Securities plc and non-executive director on the board of SymphonyAI. She has previously served on numerous other boards including A.P. Moeller Maersk, Credit Suisse, Santander Consumer USA, Forge, and GCM Grosvenor.

Blythe also has significant experience in nonprofit governance, having served as the co-chair of the Global Fund for Women, vice chair of ID2020, chair of the NYC chapter of Susan G. Komen Breast Cancer Foundation, chair of the Hyperledger Foundation, and numerous other trustee roles.

Blythe takes over the Chair from Sir John Lazar who has led the Board of Trustees since 2020. Under Sir John’s leadership the Foundation has supported hundreds of thousands of educators and tens of millions of students all over the world to develop the skills, knowledge, and mindsets to shape their world through computing and AI.

We have achieved so much under his leadership and I have learned a huge amount from working with him. We are all profoundly grateful to Sir John for his contribution. 

Blythe will take up the role at the end of March 2027 and John will be staying on to manage the transition and handover. While it is hard to imagine a world where John isn’t our Chair, I am genuinely excited about the prospect of working with Blythe.

What is a Board of Trustees?

As a charity, the Foundation is governed by a Board of Trustees that is responsible for ensuring we use our resources effectively to advance our charitable goals. We are fortunate to have an exceptionally strong and diverse group of Trustees who bring significant experience and expertise from a wide range of backgrounds. Trustees generally serve two three-year terms. Trustees are volunteers who provide their time and expertise to the Foundation for no remuneration. 

You can see the full list of Trustees and Members on our website.

The post The next Chair of the Board of Trustees, Blythe Masters appeared first on Raspberry Pi Foundation.

The post From musical fruit to walking robots: Coolest Projects India returns to Hyderabad appeared first on Raspberry Pi Foundation.
item.content:encoded:
Coolest Projects returned for its second year in India on Saturday 19 September, taking place in Telangana’s state capital Hyderabad once more.

This year’s India event brought together 326 young technology creators who showcased 132 projects: India’s young tech creator community is clearly growing stronger. From AI to hardware to the web, young people’s projects took on topics that mattered to them, covering the playful to the practical.

A showcase of standout ideas

Here are just a few of the creative projects young people shared on the day.

Vhedhya, Tanvi, Bhavani, and Sameeksha | Fruit keys — Advanced programming

Fruit keys is a project that turns fruit into a musical instrument. The team used a Raspberry Pi computer, a camera, and the software library OpenCV. Bananas work as virtual keys that trigger musical notes. An apple lets players switch between instrument sounds. It’s a fun example of how computer vision can create touch-free, interactive experiences.

Kumari, Bhoomika, and Shaurya | Kinetic care — Hardware

Kinetic care is a smart physical therapy system for use at home. A camera tracks the user’s movements, so they can play a therapy-based video game while they exercise. A wearable sensor watches for sudden or unsafe muscle movements. If it spots one, it sends a vibration alert straight away to help prevent injury. The project shows how hardware can make rehabilitation safer and more engaging.

Srishti, Kimaya | Chrome dino in real life — Games

This is a dinosaur-themed game with a motorised conveyor, moving obstacles, and increasing difficulty. Players dodge obstacles using a button while LEDs and sound effects create an arcade experience. High scores unlock rewards!

A day to remember

Bringing Coolest Projects to India for a second year showed us just how much creativity and ambition exists among young people here. Every project represented hours of learning, problem-solving, and imagination, and it’s a privilege to give these creators a platform to be seen and celebrated.

Events like this shine a light on why investing in young people’s digital skills matters so much for India’s future. 

What stood out to us most this year was the breadth of ideas on display, and the confidence with which these young tech creators presented their work. It’s a strong signal of where India’s next generation of creative thinkers and problem-solvers is heading.

A huge thank you to our partner Code Club India for their support with this event, to the volunteers and mentors who made the day possible, and to our sponsors Qube Research and Technologies. And most of all we want to thank every young creator who showed up ready to share and connect with their community. We can’t wait to see what you build next.

Want to get involved?

There are still a few partner-run Coolest Projects events to come this year — find out if there is one near you. Want to be the first to hear about announcements for 2027? Sign up to the Coolest Projects newsletter for dates, deadlines, and updates.

item.title: How classroom challenges can change how students see computing
item.dc:creator: Dan Fisher
item.description:
Computing education in England is in a stronger position than it was a decade ago. Increased access to technology, free learning resources for young people, and improved training for computing teachers has put us on a path to success.  But the subject is also at an important inflection point. Young people are growing up in…

The post How classroom challenges can change how students see computing appeared first on Raspberry Pi Foundation.
item.content:encoded:
Computing education in England is in a stronger position than it was a decade ago. Increased access to technology, free learning resources for young people, and improved training for computing teachers has put us on a path to success. 

But the subject is also at an important inflection point. Young people are growing up in a world shaped by digital technologies like AI, yet not all young people get the same opportunities to discover how computing can be creative, collaborative, and relevant to their lives. This is reflected in the number of learners who choose to study it. In England, GCSE Computer Science entries fell by 4.7% in summer 2025 (93,980 to 89,610), and A level entries fell by 2.4% (19,475 to 19,010)*. 

Creating positive, accessible experiences early in a students’ education, and helping them to build confidence and see computing as something they can engage with, has never been more important.

For educators, computing is about much more than preparing learners for a single subject or qualification. Skills England’s 2025 assessment of priority skills up to 2030 estimates that demand for priority occupations will grow by 0.9 million, including 87,000 additional programmers and software development professionals**. These roles are identified as a priority across seven industry sectors, underlining the value of the broader skills students develop through computing: problem-solving, logical reasoning, creativity, and confidence.

That’s why initiatives such as the UK Bebras Challenge and the Raspberry Pi Foundation Coding Challenge matter. They give teachers ready-made, engaging ways to introduce computational thinking and coding without needing students to already see themselves as ‘computer scientists’. Low-barrier, fun, and practical, they help students experience the satisfaction of solving problems for themselves. As Mitchel Resnick, Professor of Learning Research at the MIT Media Lab, puts it: “They are not just learning to code, they are coding to learn.”***

Over the past year, the UK Bebras Challenge (November 2025), and the Raspberry Pi Foundation Coding Challenge (March 2026), have reached hundreds of thousands of students across the UK.

Participation continues to grow. In 2025, 562,924 students took part in Bebras, up from 467,000 in 2024, contributing over 1 million hours of learning. The Coding Challenge also grew, with 85,389 students taking part in 2026, up from 83,096 in 2025.

To understand what this looks like at the grassroots level, we spoke to two teachers about why they run these challenges and what their students gain from taking part.

Johanna Watkins, Head of Computer Science at Highcliffe School, on the UK Bebras Challenge

What made you decide to take part in the UK Bebras Challenge?

I was introduced to the Bebras Challenge during my teacher training, where my placement school was already taking part in the competition. Not only was it an affordable way to introduce students to the world of computational thinking, but I quickly realised how useful it was in identifying which students would be a good fit for GCSE Computer Science. Since my initial positive experience, I’ve ensured that all computer science students take part in the challenge, no matter which school I’ve worked in.

What makes Bebras different from other activities or competitions?

From an admin perspective, it is quick and easy to create accounts for a large number of students in one go. Once student data is downloaded from your MIS, importing the spreadsheets is incredibly simple. As a busy teacher, this saves me a lot of time.

For students, the accessibility of Bebras is a big selling point. Due to the on-screen reader, ability to add extra time for SEND students and differentiated challenges, everyone can access the competition. The interactive elements within the questions also make it engaging and enjoyable to work with.

How do students usually respond when they first encounter Bebras tasks?

Students can be easily influenced by their teachers. When introducing the Bebras Challenge every year, it’s important to clarify its purpose and the reason behind taking part. With a genuine motive explained, I find students are receptive to attempting something new. Every individual challenge is unique and colourful, operating a simple UI to jump between questions. Students are spurred on to get stuck into the puzzles on their first encounter, responding to the tasks with confidence.

What skills do you think students develop through Bebras?

The number one skill that students develop is their ability to problem-solve. When faced with tasks of varying difficulties, they are able to apply the key principles of abstraction and decomposition to tackle problems. If I’m with a GCSE or A Level class, it presents as the perfect opportunity to reinforce their theory knowledge, linking computational thinking concepts to the question in front of them.

Additionally, it can promote the hard skill of literacy. By having separate competitions for different year groups, students are reading texts that are of an appropriate level for their age bracket. And if you’re in a primary school, there’s the option to work in groups, allowing students to develop another soft skill of teamwork.

Can you share a specific example of a student benefiting from the challenge?

I’ve previously taught a Year 9 student with a reading age of 10, who was finding all aspects of school a challenge. Utilising the adaptive technology available to them in the Bebras Challenge, they were one of few in their class to achieve a Merit. This student was able to showcase their strong logical reasoning skills, without being hindered by their reading comprehension.

Consequently, they chose Computer Science as one of their GCSE options and wanted to pursue a career as a software developer. It also raised an interesting discussion point with the school, investigating various access arrangements to better support them. The Bebras Challenge has quite literally changed this student’s life.

What advice would you give to a teacher wanting to run the challenge in their school?

Just go for it! Given how renowned the competition is, my sixth form students have mentioned their results in university and apprenticeship applications. If students are needing evidence to back up their problem-solving abilities, or wanting to differentiate themselves from others with similar grades, the UK Bebras Challenge gives them an extra string to their bow.

As a teacher, just make sure you’re organised and prepare the accounts well in advance. Once the student accounts have all been created, using the helpful Coordinator Handbook as guidance, you can export their details and create login slips. Coupled with Bebras’ instructions presentation for in-class, it made for a smooth set-up and delivery. As the competition is straight after October half-term, it also allows teachers to ease their way back into school life. We always look forward to Bebras week at my school!

Isobel Culmer, Teacher of Computer Science at Barton Peveril School, on the Raspberry Pi Foundation Coding Challenge

How did you first get involved with the Coding Challenge?

We are always looking for more competitions for students to participate in. We run a few competitions, but most are for the elite only. For example, we run the British Informatics Olympiad and British Algorithmic Olympiad but only about 20 of our 340 students can attempt either.

So when we heard about the Coding Challenge, it was exactly what we were looking for, a competition where everyone could take part and achieve good results. It’s always good to practise more coding skills, so this competition is ideal for us. This year was the first time we had the whole cohort take part, both Year 12 and Year 13.

How do students usually respond when they first encounter the Coding Challenge tasks?

The vast majority of students are excited about the Coding Challenge. They love competition!

The very first time they see them, it can be a bit overwhelming. There is a lot to do in a short time, which is why we get students to practise before the actual competition.

The emphasis of this challenge is firmly on coding compared to the computational thinking focus on the Bebras Challenge. Why is coding still an important skill to teach learners?

It has always been about problem solving. This is a skill that is still very much in demand, perhaps more so now. We are still teaching computational thinking when teaching them to code. There are many transferable skills from learning to code that are useful in most careers and industries. The need for resilience and attention to detail are vital skills for all.

Besides specific coding skills, what other skills do you think students develop through the Coding Challenge?

It develops resilience and many other skills such as following instructions precisely, which are important in life. Also time management and planning, students need to decide what to try and in what order if they want to maximise their score.

Can you share any examples of a student or group doing something in the Challenge that ignited their interest in computing?

Quite a few students will continue to work on the problems they encountered after the challenge has finished. They are determined to solve the problems! I hear many groups discussing techniques they used to solve the trickier problems which gives them the confidence to use those techniques in their classwork.

What advice would you give to a teacher wanting to run the Challenge in their school?

Do it! It is so easy to do. We run it in a normal lesson; it is in our schedule of lessons so all teachers do it the same week. From two weeks before the day we choose to set the challenge, we set homework to be practice questions.

The tricky part is making sure the students understand the interface, what code to copy in and how to test and run it, so the homework gives them a chance to do this. One teacher sets up the spreadsheet with all the student names to import to the very easy-to-use teacher admin website. It is then easy to download each class’s usernames and passwords.

Making computing accessible at scale

Across both challenges, one thing is clear: when barriers are lowered, more students take part and discover that computing is for them. Whether through short problem-solving tasks or coding challenges, these experiences build confidence, develop transferable skills, and help learners see themselves in computing.

For teachers, they also offer something equally important: practical, structured activities that can fit into the school year and work with whole classes or cohorts. In a landscape where the UK needs more young people to develop digital and computational skills, accessible challenges like these can help spark interest early, celebrate success, and give every learner a meaningful first step into computing.

How to get involved

To register your school for the next UK Bebras Challenge coming in November 2026, go to bebras.uk.

**https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/assessment-of-priority-skills-to-2030/assessment-of-priority-skills-to-2030

***https://web.media.mit.edu/~mres/papers/L2CC2L-handout.pdf

The post Not all explanations are equal: Social Explainable AI and Critical Computational Literacy appeared first on Raspberry Pi Foundation.
item.content:encoded:
AI technologies, such as smart speakers or streaming recommendations, are becoming part of everyday life for children and teenagers. It’s therefore increasingly important to help young people understand not just how these systems work, but how to question them.

When AI systems generate outputs such as a recommendation, these outputs are often accompanied by an explanation. In our latest research seminar, Professor Dr. Dan Verständig (Goethe University Frankfurt, Center for Critical Computational Studies) spoke about how explanations are shaped by the people who write them, and only become meaningful when someone else makes sense of them. Dan introduced us to Social Explainable AI (Social XAI) and Critical Computational Literacy (CCL), and asked us to consider not just what an AI system explains, but for whom, why, and who benefits.

Why do we need explanations?

Dan opened with a deceptively simple question: why do we need explanations in the first place? His answer was that explanations provide orientation. They reduce uncertainty, and in doing so, they make our shared social world liveable. Explanations have evolved from Socratic dialogue, to the printed book, to the classroom, to today’s digital interfaces, and now to AI-generated explanations. But explanations have never been neutral conveyors of information. Dan illustrated this with a simple demonstration: he showed the seminar participants an aerial photo of a beach and asked what they noticed.

The aerial photo Dan shared during his seminar. What do you notice about this picture?

Seminar participants pointed to the coastline, the sandy beach, and a tiny figure in the frame. Dan then revealed that the photo was taken by him, using a drone at Montara State Beach in California on a specific afternoon in April 2024. He asked how a climate researcher, a surfer, or an artist might each describe the very same image differently.

This demonstration highlighted that an explanation is always for someone, for some purpose, in some context. That framing carries straight through into how we should think about AI explanations too. An explanation that satisfies a data scientist debugging a model is not the same as one that satisfies a patient asking why an algorithm flagged their scan, or a citizen asking why they were denied a loan. In other words, explanations are never technical.

From delivering explanations to co-constructing them

Drawing on Rohlfing and Lim’s 2026 work, Dan described Social XAI as an approach that puts interaction, rather than output, at the centre of explainability. Dan illustrated this with a simple but effective diagram: an AI explanation starts as a system output, is filtered through a person’s interpretation, and only then becomes meaning through construction. A one-size-fits-all output, however technically accurate, isn’t yet an explanation until someone has made sense of it in their own terms.

To explore this further, Dan’s research group has developed co-construction workshops, bringing people together to interrogate AI explanations collaboratively rather than receive them passively. In these workshops, participants are asked questions such as: “What counts as evidence? What is missing? What are the alternatives? Who benefits from this? Do we agree?”

To answer these questions, participants do not examine an AI model to find out how it generates a decision. Instead, participants scrutinise its outputs in the same way that they would critically evaluate a politician’s promise or a newspaper’s headline. 

Dimensions for engaging critically with explanations

Critical Computational Literacy (CCL) is a framework that describes what people need to engage with AI explanations critically. Dan presented CCL as consisting of four interlocking dimensions:

  • Attitude — a critical stance and value awareness: approaching computational systems not as neutral tools but as artefacts that embed particular values and assumptions
  • Biography — recognising that people’s relationships with technology are shaped by subjectivity, by the varied encounters they’ve had with computational systems, and by the diverse pathways that brought them to this point
  • Capacity — the analytical, creative, and ethical skills needed to actually work with and through computational systems, not just talk about them
  • Critique — the capacity that ties the other three dimensions together: asking what matters, and why

Taken together, these dimensions push back against a narrow, purely technical notion of ‘AI literacy’ as knowing how a model works. Instead, CCL treats literacy as something biographical and value-laden. Dan explained that individuals bring their own history and stance to any encounter with computational systems, and genuine literacy means being able to interrogate these systems’ explanations rather than simply accept or operate them.

Using these ideas in your classroom

Although Dan’s research took place with adult participants, Social XAI and Critical Computational Literacy are ideas that could also be used in the K-12 classroom. For example, if students interact with AI explanations through smart speakers or streaming recommendations in their everyday lives, this presents an opportunity to teach them how to engage critically with AI outputs. Students might explore why a smart speaker suggested a particular recipe, or investigate the explanation for why a streaming service recommended a particular show. 

Explainability is also a key part of our own Experience AI resources. When training a model, students write their own model cards to document who built a model, what training data was used, how accurate the model’s predictions were, and any known limitations. In this activity, explainability is traceable, and students use their analytical skills to create transparent, fair, and accountable model cards.

Social XAI suggests an extension to this activity. Students could ask what matters about the explanation they have written and why this is important. Through this critique, students can consider who will read these model cards and how the cards might be interpreted. In this way, AI explanations become more than a technical output, and become artefacts whose meaning is co-constructed by the author and the reader. 

This seminar was part of our ongoing series on teaching about AI in the arts, humanities, and sciences. You can watch the full recording of Dan’s talk, including the Q&A discussion, here:

Join our next seminar

Our research seminar series continues to explore how AI is taught across the curriculum. In our next seminar on Tuesday, 6 October at 19:00–20:30 BST, we welcome Eleni Petraki and Damith Herath (University of Canberra) who will present an engineering and robotics curriculum aimed at equipping future engineers with the diverse skills demanded by a growing workforce. To take part in the seminar, click the button below to register. We hope to see you there.

Register for the next seminar

The schedule of our upcoming seminars is available online. You can catch up on past seminars on the blog and on the previous seminars and recordings page.

item.content:encoded:
Imagine this scenario:

Alex, a teenaged learner, reads a homework assignment, ponders a little, and then opens an AI chatbot. A quick prompt produces a structured, well-written answer within seconds. Alex pastes the text into a document, tweaks a few words, and submits the work.

For many young people, this is becoming the norm.

Recent reports show that, in countries including the US and UK, over half of all teens use AI tools for homework, and 1 in 10 says they do most or all of their homework with chatbots. “I use it every day,” stated one 17-year-old student in a recent study (Pew Research, 2026), and went on to say how she relies on chatbots for everything from homework to life decisions. In another study, a teenager openly admitted to using AI to cheat on assignments, essays, and book reports (Harvard GSE, 2024).

This raises an important question: when AI technology does the work, what happens to the learning?

Researchers are increasingly concerned that such uncritical use of AI tools may lead to cognitive offloading, where learners outsource their thinking, and the weakening of higher-order thinking skills in young people, such as problem-solving, critical thinking and creativity.

To address these concerns, the Raspberry Pi Foundation and Google DeepMind have teamed up to create a new unit of research-informed lessons on large language models (LLMs) as part of Experience AI. Rather than focusing simply on how to use AI tools, the new unit helps learners understand how LLMs work, evaluate their outputs, and use them strategically to support their own learning.

The unit, designed for 13- to 16-year-old learners, supports a learning-focused approach, drawing on metacognition, critical thinking, feedback literacy, and learning-centered prompt engineering. The five lessons in it support young people’s cognitive development, strengthen their metacognitive skills, and bolster their ability to strategically use LLMs for their learning. They draw on extensive research within Google DeepMind’s Learning team on how to scaffold around AI use to preserve ‘productive struggle’ and learner agency.

Research-informed pedagogies

Feedback literacy: Developing learners’ judgement of AI-generated outputs

The new ‘Using LLMs strategically for learning’ unit is grounded in learning science research, including feedback literacy. Feedback literacy refers to the skill of actively interpreting, judging and using information when learning, instead of passively receiving information. 

In the unit, learners explore three types of information, also called ‘feedback types’:

  • Telling: When someone is given the answer straight away
  • Guiding: When someone is guided with hints
  • Challenging: When someone is asked questions that make them think harder

Learners discover that deep learning requires a blend of all three feedback types. They also analyse LLM outputs and discover that LLMs default to providing the answer, usually in a ‘tell’ format. 

To help learners strategically use LLMs for their learning, they are provided with prompting strategies that elicit LLM outputs in ‘guide’ and ‘challenge’ formats. This helps learners engage more deeply with their own learning and develop higher-order thinking skills.

Prompting techniques for learning, not just answers

To help young people strategically use LLMs for their learning, the lessons include learning-centred, platform-agnostic prompting techniques. These include strategies borrowed from research papers on the most effective prompting frameworks. To make sure that the prompting strategies in the lessons remain effective over time and can be translated into different languages when we expand the resources, we did not use acronyms, unlike most popular prompting frameworks.

Building metacognition and future-ready skills

There are several industry reports highlighting the future-proof skills in the age of AI, such as problem solving, communication, critical thinking, collaboration and creativity skills. In the ‘Large language models’ unit, learners reflect on which skills they want to build and consider how their use of LLMs can support or hinder their development, helping them make responsible and intentional choices about using LLMs in ways that build their long-term capabilities rather than replace them.

There are also activities in the lesson resources that help learners understand the long-term impacts of cognitive offloading and uncritical LLM use on the development of their future skills. The resources encourage learners to stay actively engaged in their learning and be reflective of their LLM use when learning.

Uncovering LLM training data

Many young people (Pew Research, 2026) use LLMs as search engines, believing that LLMs produce outputs that are always accurate. To address that misconception, the lessons include activities that question where the training data comes from, and how accurate those sources of data are. 

For example, when young people discover that a portion of data that LLMs are trained on come from social media platforms like Reddit and Facebook, they are encouraged to question the quality and factuality of these sources through classroom-wide discussions. Through discussions and thinking exercises, learners are also encouraged to question whose voices, languages, cultures and perspectives are (and are not) represented in these AI models.

Looking ahead

As AI tools become more integrated in young people’s lives, many learners, like Alex, are tempted to turn to AI tools for quick answers, convenience, and support. 

The ‘Using LLMs strategically for learning’ unit equips young people with the skills to use LLMs effectively, critically and strategically, in ways that are most helpful to their learning. Through research-informed lessons, they explore how LLMs are created, why their outputs are not always accurate and how to evaluate AI-generated responses. 

Just as importantly, learners are encouraged to reflect on their own use of AI: when using an LLM supports their learning, when it does not, and how they can remain in control of their thinking, learning and skills development.

With these resources, young people like Alex are not discouraged from using LLMs, but encouraged to pause, rewrite their prompts in ways that are more helpful to their learning, evaluate the outputs they receive, and stay actively involved in their own thinking. 

As we prepare young people for a future we do not yet know, the most important skill we can teach them is how to keep thinking. Who does the thinking, gets the learning.

The unit is available on the Experience AI website.

Acknowledgements

We would like to thank all the educators across South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, the United Kingdom, India and beyond who piloted these resources and shared their thoughtful feedback. Their contributions helped shape and strengthen the unit. We are also grateful to Google DeepMind for their continued support in the development of this unit.
